seo_title: Spinal Stenosis Treatment in North Palm Beach | First Rehab
seo_desc: Lumbar spinal stenosis treatment in North Palm Beach. One-on-one physical therapy to help you stand and walk longer with less leg pain. Medicare accepted.
lede: Physical therapy for lumbar spinal stenosis that helps you walk farther, stand longer and stay active, with exercise matched to how your back and legs respond.
what_it_is: Your spinal canal is the tunnel of bone that protects the nerves running down your back. Stenosis means this space has narrowed and crowds those nerves. According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, discs lose water and height with age, which puts more load on the small joints of the spine. Those joints develop arthritis and bone spurs, and nearby ligaments thicken, together taking up room the nerves need.

Lumbar spinal stenosis is mainly a condition of later life. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons notes that up to 95% of people show some degenerative changes in the spine by age 50, and that stenosis usually develops after 60, affecting men and women equally. Mayo Clinic reports most people with spinal stenosis are older than 50. Some people are born with a narrower canal and notice symptoms earlier.
symptoms: Pain, cramping or heaviness in one or both legs when you stand or walk
Leg symptoms that ease when you sit down or bend forward
Burning pain in the buttocks that spreads into the legs
Numbness or tingling in the buttocks, legs or feet
Leg weakness or a foot that catches or drags
Walking that feels easier while leaning on a shopping cart
Low back pain that may come and go
causes: Arthritis of the spinal joints and the bone spurs it produces
Discs that lose height and bulge with age
Thickened, stiff ligaments inside the spinal canal
A herniated disc pressing into the canal
Being born with a narrow spinal canal
A previous spine injury, such as a fracture from a car accident

how_therapy_helps.intro: The APTA ChoosePT guide states that in most cases, symptoms of spinal stenosis can be effectively managed with physical therapy and other conservative treatments. A randomized trial led by physical therapist Anthony Delitto, published in Annals of Internal Medicine in 2015, compared a standardized physical therapy program with decompression surgery and reported similar results, according to ChoosePT. StatPearls lists stretching, strengthening and aerobic fitness among first-line conservative care, with the goal of keeping you walking and active.
methods: Because bending forward tends to open space for the nerves, your therapist teaches movements and resting positions that use that posture to ease leg symptoms.
ChoosePT notes that bicycling may suit people with stenosis better than walking, since walking is usually more painful than sitting. Building fitness raises how long you can stay on your feet.
Stronger abdominal, back, hip and thigh muscles help support the spine and take some of the workload off the arthritic joints.
Stretching tight hip flexors and improving lower back motion can make standing upright more comfortable.
You learn how to pace walks, use brief sitting breaks and adjust how you stand and walk to relieve pressure on the nerves.

first_visit: Your first visit runs about an hour. Your therapist asks how far you can walk or how long you can stand before leg symptoms begin, and what brings relief. You may mark painful and numb areas on a body diagram. The exam includes muscle strength and sensation testing, posture and walking observation, range of motion of the spine and legs, and hands-on assessment of joint mobility. Treatment and a home program start the same day.
recovery: Lumbar spinal stenosis is usually a long-term condition, so the aim of therapy is to manage symptoms and keep you moving. Its course varies: StatPearls notes that while some people improve over time, most see the condition gradually progress, and there is no standard recovery timeline. Many people find they can walk and stand longer once they are exercising consistently and using the positions that relieve their legs. Keeping up a home program after discharge helps protect those gains.
self_care: Sit down or lean forward when leg symptoms build during a walk, then continue
Try a stationary bike, or walk while leaning on a shopping cart
Keep moving every day in short, comfortable bouts
Limit long periods of standing upright and walking downhill
see_a_doctor: Loss of bladder or bowel control (seek emergency care)
Numbness in the genital or saddle area
Leg weakness that is quickly getting worse
New or rapidly worsening numbness in the legs

faqs.q: Can spinal stenosis be treated without surgery?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. The APTA ChoosePT guide states that in most cases spinal stenosis symptoms can be effectively managed with physical therapy and other conservative treatments, and that only the most severe cases need surgery or spinal injections. Conservative care focuses on exercise, positions that relieve pressure on the nerves and building walking tolerance. Your physician decides with you if surgery becomes necessary.

faqs.q: Why does spinal stenosis hurt more when I walk?
faqs.a: Standing and walking upright arch the lower back slightly, which narrows the space around the nerves further. StatPearls describes this pattern, called neurogenic claudication: pain worsens with standing, walking and leaning back, and improves with sitting or bending forward. It also notes many people tolerate walking uphill better than downhill for the same reason.

faqs.q: What exercises should I avoid with spinal stenosis?
faqs.a: Movements that arch the lower back for long periods tend to aggravate symptoms. StatPearls advises avoiding downhill walking and excessive backward bending. That does not mean avoiding exercise. The APTA ChoosePT guide notes that some exercises suit stenosis better than others, and a physical therapist can show you which ones to use and which to hold off on.

faqs.q: Is physical therapy as effective as surgery for spinal stenosis?
faqs.a: For some patients, research suggests it can be comparable. According to the APTA ChoosePT summary, a 2015 randomized trial in Annals of Internal Medicine compared standardized physical therapy with decompression surgery and found similar results, while surgery carried a higher complication risk. An accompanying editorial suggested patients be offered a rigorous physical therapy program. Every case differs, so discuss options with your physician.

faqs.q: Does spinal stenosis get worse over time?
faqs.a: It can. StatPearls notes that while some people improve with time, the majority see gradual progression. Because the narrowing is tied to age-related changes in the spine, staying strong and active is a reasonable way to help protect your walking ability, and ChoosePT notes regular exercise can help limit its impact. Rapidly worsening weakness or bladder changes need prompt medical attention.

faqs.q: Is a stationary bike good for spinal stenosis?
faqs.a: For many people it is a good fit. Sitting on a bike keeps the spine slightly bent forward, which tends to give the nerves more room. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons mentions that some people manage symptoms by using a stationary bike, and the ChoosePT guide notes bicycling may be easier than walking. Start with short, easy sessions.

notes_for_reviewer: ICD-10 M48.06 is the non-billable parent (verified on icd10data.com). Billable children: M48.061 without neurogenic claudication, M48.062 with neurogenic claudication.

The Delitto 2015 Annals of Internal Medicine trial is cited through ChoosePT's summary because PubMed blocked direct fetching. The trial had substantial crossover from PT to surgery; a clinician may want to soften or recheck the 'similar results' wording against the original abstract.
ChoosePT mentions a treadmill body-weight support harness; omitted because the brief forbids equipment claims.
No recovery timeline was found in sources, so none is stated.

Fact-check 2026-10-07: StatPearls natural-history wording restored to its meaning ('the majority have a progression'); the earlier softening misstated the source. 'Surgery' removed from causes (not in Mayo/NIAMS/ChoosePT). Saddle numbness and sudden inability to walk red flags are standard cauda equina guidance, not on the cited NIAMS page.
